newsitem.title: CROATIA: Tudjman pledges to rebuild Croatia in second term.
newsitem.headline: Tudjman pledges to rebuild Croatia in second term.

text.p: Croatia's President Franjo Tudjman declared his commitment to peace in Bosnia and pledged to rebuild his country's economy as he was sworn in for a second five-year term on Tuesday.

"I solemnly declare that I shall be an impartial president of all Croats and Croatian citizens, regardless of their political and other affiliations," Tudjman, often criticised for autocratic rule, said in his inauguration speech.

Diplomats believe he holds a firm grip on Croatia's fate and could manage to bring it closer to Western Europe, but only if he lives up to the obligations he undertook in a 1995 Balkan peace accord signed in Dayton in the United States.

Those commitments include handing over indicted Bosnian Croats to an international war crimes tribunal, allowing the return of all Serb war refugees and quelling nationalist Bosnian Croat opposition to a Croat-Moslem federation.
"We pledge our support to Dayton and the Federation," Tudjman, re-elected with a strong mandate in June, told a gathering of top state, army and church officials and foreign ambassadors.
The ceremony took place in a packed central Zagreb square on a hot summer morning, which made several people in the crowd pass out.

Tudjman will have a chance to prove Croatia's commitment to Bosnian peace on Wednesday, when he meets the Moslem chairman of Bosnia's collective presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, in the Adriatic port of Split.
The meeting, postponed several times in the last six months, will also be attended by U.S. diplomat Richard Holbrooke, who engineered the Dayton peace accord in 1995.

The 76-year-old former Yugoslav army general, reported by U.S. officials to have been treated for cancer last year, looked healthy and spoke in a firm voice, apparently confirming doctors' reports that his therapy had been successfully completed.
"We pay special attention to cooperation with the United States, the European Union... Russia, China and Islamic countries," said Tudjman, who led his country to independence from federal Yugoslavia.
He declared he would fight corruption and devote himself to the reconstruction and rebuilding of the economy, weakened by war and the loss of traditional markets in Yugoslavia.
"That will take several years, considerable financial means and the understanding of the entire nation," he said. "We shall strive to raise employment, Gross Domestic Product and living standards."

The main domestic threat to Tudjman's rule is smouldering dissatisfaction among a majority of Croats who can hardly make ends meet. The gap between rich and poor has widened as hasty privatisation has created a small, enormously wealthy elite closely linked to his ruling party.
